title: From Words to Meaning: The Neural Systems of Human Communication
kicker: Speech, Language, Reading, Writing, and Restored Communication
takeaways: Sensory word analysis, conceptual knowledge, sentence organization, and motor output can change independently; hemispheric dominance does not make language a single-center function.
Speech responses depend on the operation being performed.
Direct recordings distinguish preparation, articulation, sensory feedback, and listening; activation in motor cortex alone does not identify an articulatory code.
Compare comprehension, naming, repetition, grammar, reading, writing, and signed language to identify which transformations remain available.
Experience shapes language and literacy networks.
Early accessible language, linguistic rhythm, and writing-system experience influence neural representations; deafness and language deprivation are distinct conditions.
Reading and writing combine several routes.
Stored orthography, sound conversion, semantics, and motor sequence knowledge explain dissociations among acquired reading and spelling disorders.
Speech, handwriting, and cursor decoders use preserved intentional signals; restoring a motor route differs from repairing lost word meanings or grammatical knowledge.
